# 02 — What you fear losing

**This is the row that decides who moves.** Machiavelli's actual observation is that people work
harder to protect what they have than to gain what they do not. Whoever has more at risk in a
specific exchange is the one who gives ground.

Most people fill in "what I want" honestly and then write this one as if nothing worries them.
That produces confident advice built on a map that is wrong in the only place it matters.

---

## What you would genuinely hate to lose

Be honest. Nobody reads this but you and the skill.

| At risk | How badly | Who could take it |
|---|---|---|
| [e.g. this client's monthly retainer] | [it is 40% of revenue] | [them, on 30 days notice] |
| [e.g. your reputation with a particular audience] | [severe, slow to rebuild] | [a public disagreement] |
| [e.g. a relationship that introduces you to others] | [moderate] | [souring one deal] |
| [e.g. time — the deal is eating hours you do not have] | [high] | [saying yes] |

## What you can genuinely walk away from

The other half, and the more useful one. Anything here is a place you can be firm without
bluffing.

- [e.g. any single brand deal — none is more than 8% of revenue]
- [e.g. work that arrives below rate]

## The things you are afraid of that are NOT actually risks

Write these down, because they are the ones that make you concede for nothing.

- [e.g. "they will tell people I am difficult" — they will not, and if they do, nobody cares]
- [e.g. "this is the only offer I will get this quarter" — check whether that is true]

## Your calibration — the part everyone skips

Most people are consistently off in ONE direction. Knowing which one is worth more than any
tactic in the skill.

> [Do you under-ask or over-reach? Do you avoid conflict or seek it? Do you discount to close, or
> hold out too long? Write the honest answer.]

**If you under-ask:** the correction is *ask for more, sooner* — never *agree to more*. Those are
opposite things and confusing them is how "be bolder" turns into "say yes to everything".

**If you over-reach:** the correction is *check the ground before you push* — their budget cycle,
their boss, whether they have already committed internally.

## What you have said no to before, and what happened

Evidence beats theory. Two or three lines.

- [e.g. "Turned down a $500 sponsorship in March. Nothing bad happened. They came back in June at
  $2,000."]
